segments.section: A model that participates in a decision
segments.text: Micah's proposal begins with a recognizable difference between knowing a religious statement and using it while acting. A person can repeat a teaching without bringing it to bear on their own conduct. In the Cognitive Gnosticism discussion, he suggests that a sufficiently present model of Jesus supplies something more active: an example against which a person can compare their response.

segments.section: A model that participates in a decision
segments.text: He writes that a person can change once they have a model in their mind of who Jesus was, what he did and what he said. The comparison with gradient descent identifies a direction of change. Instead of treating moral development as an unexplained leap, the proposal asks what representation supplies the standard and what discrepancy initiates an adjustment.
What the analogy actually contributes

The analogy can be unpacked without pretending that an equation has been measured in a believer's brain. An encounter produces a possible response. The inward example makes an alternative response available. The person notices the difference, revises their action or rehearses a different one, and carries the result into a later encounter. This sequence is an editorial explanation of the proposal, not an experimentally established learning rule.

Its strength is specificity: the content of the model matters. A model centered on mercy, a model centered on punishment and a model centered on institutional obedience could guide very different choices. Calling all three religious does not make their effects identical. Antichrist as a pattern of conduct asks how that difference becomes an ethical judgment about authority.

segments.section: Interpretation is part of the mechanism
segments.text: The archive does not contain one unchanging account of Jesus. Micah compares canonical and Gnostic portrayals, asks whether inherited interpretations have distorted earlier teaching, and explores inward readings of spiritual ascent. The inward model is therefore also an object of criticism. A person can revise what they believe the example asks of them, not merely become more efficient at obeying it.

segments.section: Interpretation is part of the mechanism
segments.text: This creates an important feedback question for Cognitive Gnosticism: what corrects a model that is vivid and motivating but morally mistaken? A mechanism of self-adjustment cannot answer that question simply by showing that adjustment occurred. The content of the teaching and the consequences for other people remain essential.

segments.section: A question that can become more concrete
segments.text: A developed study would distinguish remembering teachings, imagining a moral exemplar, noticing a conflict and changing a decision. It would compare the claimed mechanism with other explanations rather than infer a brain process from a shared metaphor. The archive supplies the proposal and its vocabulary; further work must supply that discriminating evidence.

segments.section: A question that can become more concrete
segments.text: The practical insight remains clear even before such a study: an example can become part of how a person evaluates themselves. The theological and scientific questions concern what that example is, why it has authority and how its effects should be understood.

segments.section: A worked decision, including correction of the model
segments.text: Imagine a community editor who receives a hostile but partly accurate criticism. The first impulse is to discredit its author. The editor brings to mind an image of Christ that emphasizes truthful judgment and care for the neighbor. That image makes another response possible: separate the accurate observation from the insult, correct the mistake, and refuse to turn the exchange into punishment of the critic. This is a conceptual example of Micah's proposed mechanism, not a measured clinical intervention.

segments.section: A worked decision, including correction of the model
segments.text: The next encounter reveals a limitation. Suppose the editor has also learned that being merciful means never setting a boundary. A critic then begins harassing someone else. Mere consistency with the original model would now perpetuate harm. The editor must revise the understanding of mercy so that care includes protection and accountability. Moral learning thus has two levels: adjusting conduct to a standard and revising the interpretation of the standard.

segments.section: A worked decision, including correction of the model
segments.text: That second level is indispensable. Otherwise the model could make a person more efficient at implementing a mistaken ideal. The will comparison adds another test: does the model ever challenge what the person wants, or does it always provide a sacred justification for it? The difference between God's will and personal desire cannot operate if the individual defines the former to agree with the latter in every case.

segments.section: A historical teacher and a living representation
segments.text: The Thomas and Teacher inquiry asks how sayings, communities and authority might have survived across generations. The inner-model account asks how a received portrayal participates in present action. These can interact: recovering a neglected teaching may change the model through which someone judges themselves. They do not have to be the same claim. A representation's present influence does not establish its historical author's identity, and an unresolved historical identity does not make the representation psychologically inert.

segments.section: A historical teacher and a living representation
segments.text: Micah's source links inward reception to a more general inquiry into interpretation, not simply admiration for a famous person. Which sayings supply the standard? Who controls access to them? Which inherited readings make domination appear sacred? These questions connect the individual example to the social history of an inheritance rather than treating the mind as isolated from culture.
Fidelity is not uncritical imitation

A demanding model permits uncomfortable correction. It may require admitting an error to an opponent, refusing a group's demand for cruelty, or relinquishing a claim to special authority. It also permits examination of its teachers. A leader cannot settle what Christ requires merely by declaring himself its authorized interpreter.

At institutional scale, a correction needs practices that survive the moment: the record of what changed, protection for those who identified the problem, and a way to revisit the conclusion. These are proposed applications connecting the inward model to repair. A brief private insight can be valuable, but it is not yet the same thing as a dependable shared capacity for better conduct.
